The story behind an idea

Stendhal syndrome: dizzy with beauty

In 1817 a writer felt palpitations leaving a church in Florence. A psychiatrist later gave it a name.

The French writer Stendhal visited the Basilica of Santa Croce in Florence in 1817, where Michelangelo and Galileo are buried. He wrote that on leaving he had palpitations and felt life draining from him, overwhelmed by so much beauty and history.

A name and many doubts

In 1979, the Florentine psychiatrist Graziella Magherini described more than a hundred tourists treated at Florence's hospital for dizziness, anxiety, depersonalisation and sometimes more serious symptoms after visiting museums. She called it Stendhal syndrome.

It does not appear in diagnostic manuals, and many experts doubt it is a distinct disorder. Travel fatigue, heat, dehydration, expectations and, in some cases, pre-existing problems probably play a part. But the experience of being moved to the point of dizziness by art is well described.

References

  1. Magherini, G. (1989). La sindrome di Stendhal. Ponte alle Grazie.
